newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada seeks deal with Mercosur trade group.
newsitem.headline: Canada seeks deal with Mercosur trade group.

text.p: Canada is seeking a deal with South American free trade bloc Mercosur, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Tuesday.

"Because the Canadian economy meshes quite well with the Mercosur countries, perhaps we could have an agreement signed between Mercosur and Canada before the completion of the free trade agreement with the rest of the Americas, including the United States," Chretien told a news conference with Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.
Mercosur is a free trade pact involving Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. Chile and Bolivia are associate members.
Canada, the United States and most of South America have agreed to work toward a free trade agreement by 2005.
But Cardoso said that talks to forge a deal between Canada and Mercosur were still in an early stage and he would not give details on how Canada would be included in the pact.
"We are just talking," Cardoso said. "What has been raised is the possibility of an understanding between Canada and Mercosur, but it's still in a vague way. We need more time to go into depth."
Cardoso, who is on a three-day state visit to Canada, said an agreement between Canada and Mercosur would be a good building block toward the Free Trade Agreement of the Americas in 2005.
A Canada-Mercosur agreement would be the second major free trade deal between Canada and South America without the participation of the United States.

Canada has free trade with Mexico through the North American Free Trade Agreement. But expansion of NAFTA to Chile has been hampered in the United States by the Republican Congress, which has refused to give President Bill Clinton fast-track authority to negotiate free trade with Chile.
Meanwhile, Canada negotiated its own free trade deal with Chile.
Chretien and Cardoso also said they hoped to increase bilateral trade.

Cardoso's visit to Canada produced an administrative arrangement for the peaceful use of nuclear energy, an agreement to exchange technical expertise and a commitment from Canada to advise Brazil in its regulation of telecommunications.
Canada's international development agency announced it would spend C$2 million ($1.4 million) to support a project promoting energy efficiency in Brazil.
Montreal-based Alcan Aluminium Ltd. also said it would invest about $350 million over the next three years to expand and modernize its aluminum rolling operations in Brazil.
Trade between Brazil and Canada was worth about C$2.5 billion ($1.79 billion) in 1996, almost double that of 1993.
